title: The Kiss
medium: Oil and gold leaf on canvas
prompts: Why is there so much gold?

sources.title: Belvedere: The Kiss
sources.text: The Kiss was painted by Gustav Klimt in 1907–08, during his Golden Phase. It shows a couple in an intimate embrace against a gold ground. Klimt used oil paint with gold and silver leaf on canvas. The square work measures 180 by 180 centimetres and is in the collection of the Belvedere in Vienna.

sources.title: Belvedere: Why did Gustav Klimt use gold?
sources.text: For Klimt, gold was an artistic device rather than simply a sign of wealth. He worked with gold leaf, silver, platinum, gold dust, and fine gold powder mixed with oil. The material changes with light and can make a painted surface feel both flat and animated. Medieval gold grounds, Byzantine mosaics, Japanese lacquer work, and East Asian art informed his use of gold. In The Kiss, the material helps make the intimate couple feel solemn, timeless, and almost sacred.

sources.title: Belvedere on Google Arts & Culture: The Kiss
sources.text: Belvedere describes The Kiss as the major work of Klimt's Golden Phase. It presents the lovers as kneeling on a flower meadow before an apparently infinite gold background. The museum notes that Klimt likely began the painting in 1907 and exhibited it in 1908 under the title Lovers. It was bought by the Austrian Ministry of Education while the exhibition was still open, and Klimt continued making changes before it was delivered, probably up to 1909. An early photograph shows changes to the lower legs and meadow in the final version.

sources.title: Smarthistory: Gustav Klimt, The Kiss
sources.text: Art historians Beth Harris and Steven Zucker describe the near-square painting as a modern icon: its gold recalls Byzantine art and helps create a cosmic, eternal setting. They note the contrast between the man's rectilinear patterns and the woman's curving circles and ovals. The bodies are largely concealed by decoration, while faces and hands carry the emotional focus. This is an interpretation rather than a settled identification of the figures.

sources.title: The Met: Gustav Klimt, Shimmer & Depth
sources.text: Klimt helped found the Vienna Secession in 1897 after leaving the conservative Vienna Artists' Association. The group promoted a new artistic outlook through exhibitions and dialogue across art forms. The Met connects Klimt's later style to Symbolism and to medieval mosaics he saw in Venice and Ravenna in 1903. The Kiss and the portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer followed as his distinctive use of shimmering surfaces developed.

sources.title: The Met: Symbolism
sources.text: Symbolist artists often used colour, form, and composition to express ideas, emotions, dreams, or visions rather than straightforward naturalistic description. The Met identifies the Vienna Secession and Klimt as an important late Central European flowering of Symbolism, and links his highly ornamental approach with Art Nouveau and the decorative arts. This context can help explain why The Kiss combines recognisable bodies with flattened, abstract-looking pattern.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Gustav Klimt
sources.text: Gustav Klimt (1862–1918) was an Austrian painter, a leading figure of Art Nouveau, and a founder of the Vienna Secession, known for flat, brilliantly coloured, decorative paintings. The Kiss, generally considered his most famous work, was painted between 1907 and 1908 using oil paint with silver, gold, and platinum leaf. Klimt's longtime companion was the fashion designer Emilie Flöge, though the two never married; he fathered several children with other women who worked as his models. The Kiss has remained in the Belvedere's collection since its purchase.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Kiss (Klimt)
sources.text: The Kiss is an oil-on-canvas painting with added gold leaf, silver, and platinum by the Austrian Symbolist painter Gustav Klimt, made in 1907–08 at the height of his 'Golden Period.' It was first exhibited in 1908 under the title Liebespaar (The Lovers), as recorded in that exhibition's catalogue, before entering the collection now held at the Österreichische Galerie Belvedere.

sources.title: Klimt-Foundation: The Biography
sources.text: Gustav Klimt was born on 14 July 1862 in Baumgarten near Vienna, the second of seven children of an engraver father and a mother with unfulfilled musical ambitions. He trained at the School of Arts and Crafts in Vienna and, with his brother Ernst and fellow student Franz Matsch, built an early career on mural commissions before developing the more personal, ornamental style that led toward works such as The Kiss.

sources.title: Google Arts & Culture: The Kiss
sources.text: Klimt never stated who the couple in The Kiss represent, but many have speculated it is a self-portrait of the artist with his lifelong companion, Emilie Flöge. One theory ties the setting to their summers together at the Attersee lake: the flower-strewn ground could stand in for its shore, and the trailing vines over the lovers' legs may echo the algae and aquatic plants found there, with the shimmering gold background suggesting sunlight scattered across the water's surface.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Emilie Louise Flöge
sources.text: Emilie Flöge (1874–1952) ran a fashion salon in Vienna with her sisters and was Klimt's closest companion for over two decades, though whether The Kiss depicts the two of them as lovers remains debated among scholars. She and Klimt were connected by family ties as well: Klimt's brother Ernst had married Emilie's sister Helene, and after Ernst's early death Klimt became guardian of their daughter, which drew him closer to the Flöge household.

sources.title: Barbican: Modern Couples — Emilie Flöge & Gustav Klimt
sources.text: The Barbican's Modern Couples exhibition material describes Flöge as Klimt's lifelong soul mate and creative collaborator rather than simply one of his many models, noting that The Kiss may well have been painted in homage to her. Flöge also helped spread Vienna Secession ideas through her own design work, running the reform-dress salon Schwestern Flöge with her sisters from 1904.

sources.title: MyModernMet: Gustav Klimt's Golden Phase
sources.text: Klimt's Golden Phase grew out of a period when he withdrew from public commissions after controversy over his University of Vienna ceiling paintings and turned toward private portraits and allegories. His incorporation of gold leaf intensified after this retreat, drawing on Byzantine mosaic traditions and producing the glistening, decorative works, including The Kiss, for which this period of his career is best known.
